query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non‐equilibrium, Mg‐containing lightweight high‐entropy alloy, thermally activated atomic diffusion leads to localized chemical segregation and the nucleation/growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds (especially at grain and phase boundaries). These newly formed phases then mediate the subsequent corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation behavior by either promoting the formation of a more adherent, protective oxide scale or by altering local oxidation kinetics relative to the initial single-phase state.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, metastable, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a nominal density below 6 g/cm³ that contains Mg along with other lightweight elements (e.g. Al, Cu, Zn, Gd) and is characterized by a suppressed equilibrium intermetallic formation.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled thermal aging or exposure in a corrosive/high-temperature oxidizing environment.
generation.conditions: Aging at temperatures sufficient to activate atomic diffusion (but below melting) and/or exposure to oxidizing media (e.g. air at elevated temperatures or corrosive electrolytes) under controlled time durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of discrete Mg-rich intermetallic phases at grain boundaries and other heterogeneities.
generation.mechanism: Due to the large differences in constituent properties and the non-equilibrium processing history, Mg diffuses more rapidly than the other elements. This causes local chemical ordering and phase separation that yield Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. These phases then alter the kinetics of oxide scale nucleation and growth, either by providing sites for the formation of a more protective, self-healing oxide film or by creating local galvanic couples that accelerate or retard oxidation and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast, metastable single-phase HEA, aged samples will show measurable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, changes in the morphology/adhesion of the oxide scale (or differences in corrosion initiation sites), and consequently altered corrosion rates and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.baseline: The initial non-equilibrium single-phase alloy state, which exhibits its inherent (baseline) corrosion and oxidation properties without significant intermetallic precipitation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ containing Mg and other elements that promote intermetallic formation; the effect is expected only when aging temperatures and exposure times are sufficient to drive diffusion-mediated phase segregation. It may not apply if the diffusion kinetics are too slow or if the composition is altered significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent to which Mg segregation controls oxide scale protectiveness versus localized attack is uncertain without systematic microstructural and electrochemical analysis. The synergy between intermetallic phase formation and oxidation kinetics might vary with subtle compositional or environmental changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples processed under non-equilibrium conditions. Subject subsets of the samples to well-controlled thermal aging treatments (varying temperature and time) and/or high-temperature corrosion/oxidation exposures. Use microstructural characterization (SEM, TEM, and XRD) to detect the evolution of Mg-rich intermetallic phases and examine the oxide scale morphology. Additionally, perform electrochemical corrosion tests and oxidation weight gain measurements to compare the aged samples to as-cast baseline specimens.
measurements: Microstructure (phase identification and grain boundary analysis via SEM/TEM/XRD)
Corrosion rate (electrochemical polarization or weight loss)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If after thermal aging or corrosion/oxidation exposure no significant formation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases (or corresponding chemical segregation) is observed and if the corrosion/oxidation behavior remains statistically identical to that of the as-cast, metastable state, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [7] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ] This well‐established mechanism highlights the central role of brittle phase precipitation and element segregation at GBs in governing embrittlement in conventional alloys.
